direct.query: What is corrective retrieval augmented generation?

documents.title: Corrective retrieval-augmented generation
documents.text: Corrective retrieval-augmented generation (CRAG) evaluates retrieved evidence before answering a question. A document grader labels each candidate relevant or irrelevant. When evidence quality is poor, the agent rewrites the query and retrieves again or uses web search. Only accepted evidence is supplied to answer generation, reducing the chance of unsupported claims.

documents.title: Conditional edges and bounded correction loops
documents.text: In a LangGraph corrective retrieval loop, grade_documents routes to generate_answer when the relevance threshold is met. Otherwise it routes to rewrite_query, followed by retrieve_again and grade_documents. Increment a retry counter when rewriting. Stop correcting once max_retries is reached. An explicit retry bound and a graph recursion limit prevent infinite loops.

documents.title: Document grading and retrieval quality
documents.text: A relevance grader checks whether each document contains information that helps answer the original question. It returns a relevant or irrelevant label and a short reason. Retrieval quality is the number of relevant documents divided by the number retrieved. An empty batch has quality zero. A configurable threshold decides whether to generate an answer or correct retrieval. This ratio is a routing heuristic, not a probability of truth.

web.question: At what temperature does water boil at the summit of Mount Everest?
web.query: boiling point of water Mount Everest summit elevation atmospheric pressure physics thermodynamics

documents.title: Boiling Point of Water at High Altitude (With Chart) | Water Calculator
documents.text:
At sea level, water boils at 212 °F (100 °C). Climb higher and that number drops steadily — to about 203 °F (95 °C) around 5,000 ft, near 193 °F (89.6 °C) at 10,000 ft, and to roughly 161.5 °F (72 °C) at the summit of Mount Everest. The cause is air pressure, not temperature itself: water boils the moment its vapor pressure equals the pressure of the air pushing down on it, and there's simply less air overhead the higher you go. Here's the full chart, the physics behind it, and what it actually [...] Water's boiling point is not a fixed 212 °F — it's a moving target set by atmospheric pressure, and atmospheric pressure falls steadily with elevation. At a mile above sea level it's already down to around 202 °F; by the summit of Everest it's barely above 160 °F. For most home cooking below about 3,000 ft the difference is negligible, but above that, longer cooking times — or a pressure cooker — make up for the cooler boil. When you need an exact figure for a specific elevation, the calculator [...] | Altitude | Boiling point (°F) | Boiling point (°C) |
| Sea level (0 ft) | 212.0 °F | 100.0 °C |
| 2,000 ft (610 m) | 208.1 °F | 97.8 °C |
| 5,000 ft (1,524 m) | 202.4 °F | 94.7 °C |
| 7,500 ft (2,286 m) | 197.8 °F | 92.1 °C |
| 10,000 ft (3,048 m) | 193.2 °F | 89.6 °C |
| Everest summit (29,032 ft) | ~161.5 °F | ~72 °C |

Figures are for pure water and the standard atmosphere. Local weather, humidity, and dissolved minerals shift the exact number by a fraction of a degree.

documents.title: Boiling point - Wikipedia
documents.text:
There are two conventions regarding the standard boiling point of water: The normal boiling point is commonly given as 100 °C (212 °F) (actually 99.97 °C (211.9 °F) following the thermodynamic definition of the Celsius scale based on the kelvin) at a pressure of 1 atm (101.325 kPa). The IUPAC-recommended standard boiling point of water at a standard pressure of 100 kPa (1 bar) is 99.61 °C (211.3 °F). For comparison, on top of Mount Everest, at 8,848 m (29,029 ft "Foot (unit)")) elevation, the [...] 8. ↑ Appendix 1: Property Tables and Charts (SI Units), Scroll down to Table A-5 and read the temperature value of 99.61 °C at a pressure of 100 kPa (1 bar). Obtained from McGraw-Hill's Higher Education website.
9. ↑ West, J. B. (1999). "Barometric pressures on Mt. Everest: New data and physiological significance". Journal of Applied Physiology. 86 (3): 1062–6. doi "Doi (identifier)"):10.1152/jappl.1999.86.3.1062. PMID "PMID (identifier)") 10066724. S2CID "S2CID (identifier)") 27875962. [...] elevation, the pressure is about 34 kPa "Pascal (unit)") (255 Torr) and the boiling point of water is 71 °C (160 °F). The Celsius temperature scale was defined until 1954 by two points: 0 °C being defined by the water freezing point and 100 °C being defined by the water boiling point at standard atmospheric pressure.

documents.title: Vapour Pressure & Why You can't Boil an Egg on Everest
documents.text:
North Ridge Pumps 30 August 2019

# Vapour Pressure & Why You can't Boil an Egg on Everest

Water boils at 100°C, correct? Well sort of. The temperature water boils at can depend on the altitude due to atmospheric pressure. The level of atmospheric pressure is dictated by altitude. Boiling is the process whereby molecules can escape from the surface of a liquid becoming a gas. [...] At sea level water boils at 100°C due to atmospheric pressure being 1.013 bar. It is possible for water to be heated above 100°C and not boil by heating water in a sealed container such as a pressure cooker. In fact, in industrial applications, it is possible for water temperatures to reach a few hundred degrees within sealed systems for heat transfer and for the generation of superheated steam. [...] As altitude increases, atmospheric pressure decreases due to the atmosphere becoming thinner. For every 300M in altitude increase the boiling temperature of water decreases by 1°C. This means at the top of Everest the boiling temperature of the water is 70°C. The reason you can not boil an egg is that an egg cooks at two different temperatures. The white cooks at 85°C and the yoke at 65°C. So on Everest, the whole of an egg will never cook.Kettles on Stove
